translations.text: After Saul died, David returned from striking down Amalek, and David stayed in Ziklag for two days.
On the third day, a man came from the camp, or from Saul’s people, with his clothes torn and dust on his head. When he ran up to David, he fell down and bowed before him to the ground.
David said to him, “Where have you come from?” He answered him, “I escaped from the camp of Israel.”
David said to him, “What has happened? Tell me.” He answered him, “The people fled from the battle, and many of the people fell and died. Saul too, and Jonathan and his sons, have died.”
David said to the young man who was telling him these things, “How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan have died?”
The young man said to David, “By chance, they happened to be on Mount Gilboa. There was Saul, leaning on his spear, and the chariots and horsemen had caught up with him.
He turned around, saw me, and called to me. I said to him, ‘Here I am.’
He said to me, ‘Who are you?’ I said to him, ‘I am an Amalekite servant.’
He said to me, ‘Stand over me and kill me, for a great darkness has covered me, and my life is not wholly within me.’

I stood over him and killed him, because I knew that he would not live after his fall. I took the crown that was on his head and the bracelet that was around his arm, and I brought them here to my lord.”
David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and all the other men who were with him tore their clothes too.
They mourned and fasted until evening for Saul, for his son Jonathan, for the people of Judah, and for the people of Israel, because they had been struck down by the sword.
David said to the young man who was telling him these things, “Where are you from?” He said, “I am the son of an Amalekite who lives as a foreigner.”
David said to him, “Were you not afraid to raise your hand against the Lord’s anointed?”
David called one of his servants and said to him, “Go up to him, strike him down, and put an end to him.” He struck him and killed him.
David said to him, “Your blood is on your own head, because your own mouth testified against you when you said, ‘I am the one who killed the Lord’s anointed.’”
David sang this lament over Saul and over his son Jonathan.
He ordered that the people of Judah be taught this lament. It is written in the Book of the Upright, or of Truth, and says:
“Stand, Israel, over those who have died, over those who were struck down on your hills. How the mighty have fallen!
Do not tell this in Gath, and do not proclaim it in the streets of Ashkelon. Do not let the daughters of the Philistines rejoice over this, or let the daughters of the uncircumcised celebrate.
Mountains of Gilboa, let no dew fall on them, and let no rain fall on you or on the choice fields, because there the shields of the warriors fell—the shield of Saul was not anointed with oil.
From the blood of those who were pierced, from the fat of the mighty, Jonathan’s bow did not turn back empty, and Saul’s bow did not turn back empty.

Saul and Jonathan, beloved and beautiful, were not separated from one another. They were beautiful in their life, and in their death too they were not separated from one another. They were swifter than eagles and stronger than lions.
Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul. Weep over the one who clothed you in scarlet with your finery, who put golden ornaments on your clothes.
How the mighty have fallen in the midst of battle! How you have fallen, Jonathan, amid the multitude of those you struck down!
I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan. You were very dear to me. Your love for me was wonderful, greater than the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen, and their weapons of war have perished!

After this, David asked the Lord, saying, “Do you want me to go up to one of the cities of Judah?” The Lord said to him, “Go up.” David said to him, “To which one shall I go up?” The Lord said to him, “Go up to Hebron.”
David went up to Hebron, with his two wives, Ahinoam the Israelite and Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.
His men who were with him, each with his household, settled in the towns of Hebron.
The men of Judah came and anointed David there to be king there over the house of Judah. David was told, “The men of Jabesh in Gilead buried Saul and Jonathan.”

Saul sent messengers to the elders of Jabesh in Gilead, saying to them, “May you be blessed by the Lord, because you showed this kindness to your lord Saul, the Lord’s anointed, by burying him and his son Jonathan.”
“Now may the Lord show you kindness and faithfulness. I too will do good to you because you have done this.
Now let your hands be strong, and be valiant men, because your lord Saul has died, and the house of Judah has anointed me to be king over them.”
Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army, took Ish-bosheth son of Saul and brought him out of the camp up to Mahanaim.
He made him king over Gilead, over Thasiri, over Israel, over Ephraim, over Benjamin, and over all Israel.
Ish-bosheth son of Saul was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he reigned for two years, except over the house of Judah, who followed David.
The time David spent in Hebron as king over the house of Judah amounted to seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul went out from Mahanaim up to Gibeon.

Joab son of Zeruiah and David’s servants, coming from Hebron, met them at the pool of Gibeon, facing one another. One group sat on one side of the pool of Gibeon, and the others sat on the other side.
Abner said to Joab, “Let the young men get up and play before us.” Joab said to him, “Let them get up.”
Twelve young men of Benjamin belonging to Ish-bosheth son of Saul got up and came into the middle, along with twelve from David’s servants.
Each seized his opponent’s head, and each thrust his sword into his opponent’s side. They fell to the ground together. That place was called “The Plotters’ Field”; it is in Gibeon.
A great and very fierce battle took place that day, and Abner and the men of Israel were defeated before David’s servants.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel was swift on his feet, like one of the gazelles in the open country.
Asahel pursued Abner. He did not turn aside from him to the right or the left, but kept running after Abner.
Abner turned around and said to him, “Is it you, Asahel, running after me?” He said, “It is I.”
Abner said to him, “Turn to your right or your left, catch one of the young men, strip him of his armor, and take it for yourself.” But Asahel would not turn aside from him in any direction.

Abner spoke to Asahel again, saying, “Turn away from me. Do not force me to strike you to the ground. How could I then lift my eyes to your brother Joab? What are you doing? Go back to your brother Joab.”

But he refused to turn away from him. Abner struck him from behind in the abdomen with his spear, and the spear pierced through him. Everyone who reached the place where Asahel had fallen and died stopped and stood still.
Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. The sun set as they reached the hill of Ammah, which is opposite Giah on the road through the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjaminites who followed Abner gathered together, joined forces, and stood on top of a single hill.

Abner called out to Joab, saying to him, “Will your sword keep devouring forever in triumph? Do you not know that it ends in bitterness? What must happen before you tell your people to stop pursuing their brothers?”
Joab said to him, “As the Lord lives, if you had not spoken, the people would have continued until morning, each pursuing his brother.”
Joab blew the trumpet, and all the people withdrew. They stopped pursuing Israel and no longer fought one another.
Abner and his men went toward the places of sunset, that is, the west, that night. They crossed the Jordan, traveled through all of Beth-horon, and came to the camp.
Joab also turned back from pursuing Abner. They gathered all the people together and found that nineteen men from David’s servants, as well as Asahel, were missing, having died.
David’s servants struck down three hundred men, by count, from the Benjaminites who followed Abner.
They took Asahel and buried him in his father’s tomb in Bethlehem. Joab and the men with him traveled all night, and dawn broke upon them at Hebron.
The war between the house of Saul and the house of David intensified. The house of David advanced and grew stronger, while the house of Saul declined and grew weaker.
Sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, the son of Ahinoam the Israelite.
His second son was Caleb [?], the son of Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. His third son was Absalom, the son of Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur.
His fourth son was Adonijah, the son of Haggith. The fifth was Shephatiah, the son of Abital.
The sixth was Ithream, the son of Eglah, David’s wife. These were born to David in Hebron.
When war arose between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner held power over the house of Saul.
Saul had a concubine named Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, said to Abner, “Why did you sleep with my father’s concubine?”

Abner became very angry because of the words of Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son. Abner said to him, “Am I a dog’s head? Today I have shown kindness to the house of Saul your father, and to your brothers and acquaintances, and I have not gone over to the house of David. Yet today you are looking for wrongdoing in me because of a woman!
May God do these things to Abner and add still more to him if I do not do for David this very day just as the Lord swore to him:
to take the kingdom away from the house of Saul and establish David’s throne over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.”
Ish-bosheth could not say anything in reply to Abner, because he was afraid of him.
Abner immediately sent messengers to David in Jerusalem, where he was, saying to him, “Make a covenant with me, and my hand will be with you to bring the whole house of Israel over to you.”
David said to him, “Good. I will make a covenant with you. But I ask one thing of you: you cannot come into my presence unless you bring Michal, Saul’s daughter, when you come to see me.”
And David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, saying to him, “Give me my wife Michal, whom I obtained for a hundred Philistine foreskins.”
Ish-bosheth sent for her and took her from her husband, Paltiel son of Selles.
Her husband walked with her, weeping as he followed her as far as Bahurim. Abner said, “Turn around and go.” So he turned around and left.
Abner spoke to the elders of Israel, saying to them, “In the past you sought David to be king over you.
Now do this, for the Lord has spoken about David, saying, ‘Through David my servant I will save Israel from the hands of the Philistines and from the hands of all their enemies.’”
Abner also spoke to the Benjaminites. Then Abner went to Hebron and told David everything that had pleased Israel and everything that had pleased the whole house of Benjamin.
Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men. David held a drinking feast for Abner and the men with him.

Abner said to David, “I will get up and go and gather Israel before my lord the king, and I will make a covenant with him. You will reign over them all as your heart desires.” David sent Abner and all the men with him away in peace.
David’s servants and Joab returned from Gedor with a great deal of plunder. Abner was not with David in Hebron, because David had sent him away, and he had gone in peace.
Joab and all his men arrived, and Joab was told, “Abner son of Ner came to David, and David sent him away, and he left in peace.”
Joab immediately went in to King David and said to him, “What have you done? Abner came to you, and why did you let him leave in peace?
Do you not know the wickedness of Abner son of Ner? He came to deceive you, to learn about your going out and coming in, and to learn everything you are going to do.”
Joab left King David’s presence and sent messengers after Abner. He brought him back from the cistern of Sirah, but David did not know.
He brought Abner back to Hebron. Joab drew him aside at the gate to speak with him, deceiving him. There he struck him in the stomach, and he died, because of the blood of Asahel, Joab’s brother.
David heard about this afterward and said, “I and my kingdom are forever innocent before the Lord of the blood of Abner son of Ner.

May these things come down upon Joab’s head and upon his father’s whole household. May Joab’s household never lack someone who is unclean, someone with leprosy, someone who holds a spindle, someone who falls by the sword, or someone who lacks bread.”
Joab and his brother Abishai had been plotting against Abner. They killed him because he had killed their brother Asahel in the battle that took place at Gibeon.
David said to Joab and to all the people with him, “Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn before Abner.” King David walked behind his bier as they carried him out.
They buried Abner in Hebron. The king raised his voice and wept at his tomb, and all the rest of the people wept for Abner.
The king sang a lament over Abner, saying, “Was Abner to die the death of Nabal?
Your hands were not bound. Your feet were not put in fetters or [?]. They sounded a trumpet for you as for a sudden calamity. He fell before lawless men.” All the people continued weeping for him.

And all the people came at the time of consolation to give David bread to eat while it was still daylight. But David swore, saying, “May God do these things to me, and add still more to them, if I eat bread or taste anything before the sun sets.”
And all the people understood, and everything the king had done pleased them.
All Israel understood that day that this decision to kill Abner had not come from the king.
And the king said to his servants, “Do you not know that a great leader has died today in Israel?
And today I am his relative, the king being the one who appointed him. But these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are far too powerful for me. May the Lord repay the evildoer according to his wickedness.”
When Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, heard that Abner had died in Hebron, his hands grew weak and he trembled. And all the people of Israel were troubled.

Two men skilled in deception belonged to Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son. One was named Baanah, and the second was named Rechab. They were sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, from the descendants of Benjamin, for Beeroth was counted among the descendants of Benjamin.
The Beerothites had fled to Gittaim and have lived there as foreigners to this day.

Jonathan, Saul’s son, had a son whose feet were disabled. He was five years old when the news about Saul and his son Jonathan was brought from Israel. His nurse picked him up and fled with him. As she was fleeing with him, he slipped away from her, fell, and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.
Rechab and Baanah, the men of Rimmon the Beerothite, went and slipped into Ish-bosheth’s house during the heat of midday. He was sleeping on his bed at noon.
The woman guarding the house was cleaning wheat, but she became drowsy and fell asleep. And Baanah and Rechab, his brothers—no one noticed them.

They slipped into the house while Ish-bosheth was sleeping on his bed in his bedroom. They struck him, killed him, and took his head. Then they went out and traveled all night along the road leading west.

They brought Ish-bosheth’s head to David in Hebron and said to the king, “Here is the head of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy who sought your life. Today the Lord has given our lord the king vengeance against your enemies in this way, against Saul your enemy and against David’s offspring.”
David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, saying to them, “As the Lord lives, who has rescued my life from every trouble,
the man who brought me the news, ‘Saul is dead,’ thought he was bringing me good news. I seized him and killed him in Ziklag, although I should have given him honors.
Now, then, wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house, on his bed. And now I will demand an accounting for his blood from you and wipe you off the earth.”

David gave orders to his servants, and they fell upon them and killed them. They cut off their hands and feet and hung them over the pool in Hebron. But they buried Ish-bosheth’s head in the tomb of Abner, the son of Ner.
All the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron, saying, “Look, we are of your bone and your flesh.

In the past, when Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought it back in. And the Lord said to you, ‘You will shepherd my people Israel, and you will be ruler over Israel.’”
All the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron. The king made a covenant with them in Hebron before the Lord, and they anointed David king over all Israel.
David was a young man, thirty years old when he became king.
He reigned over Judah in Hebron for seven years and six months, and he spent thirty-three years reigning over all Israel and Judah in Jerusalem.

And King David went with the men who were with him to Jerusalem, to the Jebusites who inhabited the land. They said to David, “You will not be able to enter this place, because [?] the blind and the lame,” saying, “David will not be able to enter this place.”
And David captured the whole fortified enclosure of Zion. This is the City of David.

And David said that day, “Whoever strikes a Jebusite, let him overcome him with a [?], and also the lame and the blind and those who hate David’s soul.” For this reason they will say, “The blind and the lame must not enter the Lord’s house.”
And David settled in the fortress and called it the City of David. He built it into a city all around, beginning at the summit of that land, together with his other house.
David grew greater every day, and the Lord Almighty was with him.
Hiram, king of Tyre, sent messengers to David, along with cedar timber, woodworkers, and workers in building stone. They built a house for David.
And David realized that the Lord had established him as king over Israel, and that his kingdom had been exalted for the sake of his people Israel.
David took more wives and concubines from Jerusalem after leaving Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David.
And these are the names of those born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon;
Eliab and Elishua, Nepheg and Japhia;
Elishama and Eliada, Shammah and Eliphelet, Jeshibath and Nathath, Elimaan and Jebarth, Joshua and Eliphalad, Naged and Nephel, Jana and Thalia, Shames and Balibath and Eliphelet.
The Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, and all the Philistines came up to search for David. David heard about it and went down to the stronghold.
The Philistines came and stationed themselves in the valley of the Rephaim.

David asked the Lord, saying, “Do you want me to go against the Philistines, and will you deliver them into my hands?” The Lord said to him, “Go up against them, for I will certainly deliver the Philistines into your hands.”

And David came out at the Heights of the Breaches and defeated the Philistines there. David said, “The Lord has broken through the Philistines before me like waters breaking through.” For this reason they named that place the Heights of the Breaches.
And they left their gods there, and David and the men with him took them away.
The Philistines came up again and stationed themselves in the valley of the giants.

David asked the Lord, saying, “Do you want me to go against the Philistines, and will you deliver them into my hands?” The Lord said to him, “Do not go up to advance against them. Turn away from them and take your position against them in front of the Place of Weeping.
And when you hear the sound of movement in the grove belonging to the Place of Weeping, then go against them, because on that day the Lord will go out ahead of you and defeat the Philistine army.”
And David did as he had commanded him. He struck the Philistines from Gibeon as far as the land of Gezer.
David again gathered all the young men in Israel, numbering seventy thousand people.

And David rose and went with all the people who were with him, from among all the rulers on the road going up, to bring from there the ark of God, over which the name of the Lord of hosts had been pronounced, who sits upon the cherubim above it.
And he placed the ark of the Lord on a new cart. They moved it from the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill, and Uzzah and his brothers, the sons of Abinadab, drove the cart
with the ark. His brothers were walking ahead of the ark.
And David and the Israelites were celebrating before the Lord with instruments, playing vigorously, and with songs, lyres, harps, drums, cymbals, and flutes.
And he came to the threshing floors of Adavid. Uzzah stretched out his hand toward the ark of God to take hold of it, because the ox had lurched aside, to steady it.
But the Lord became angry with Uzzah, and God struck him there. He died beside the ark of the Lord, before God.
David was distressed because of the blow God had inflicted on Uzzah, and he called that place “The Striking Down of Uzzah,” as it is called to this day.
David was afraid of the Lord that day and said, “How can the ark of the Lord come to me?”
David did not want the ark of the Lord’s covenant to turn toward him and enter the city of David. Instead, David diverted it to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.

The ark of the Lord remained there in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months. The Lord blessed Obed-edom’s entire household and everything he owned when the ark of the Lord entered his home.

David was told, “The Lord has blessed Obed-edom’s household and everything he owns because of the ark of the Lord.” So David went and brought the ark of the Lord out of Obed-edom’s house into the city of David in peace and with great joy.
Those carrying the ark of the Lord were singing with the choirs, and they were going to form seven choirs. There was a wonder in their chorus as they sacrificed calves and sheep.
David was playing tuned instruments before the Lord, and David was wearing a fine robe.
David and all Israel brought up the ark of the Lord with joyful shouting and the sound of a trumpet.

As the ark of the Lord was entering the city of David, Michal, Saul’s daughter, looked out through her window. She saw King David dancing and playing music before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart.
They brought in the ark of the Lord, and David set it upright in its place, in the middle of the tent that David had pitched for it. David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord.
He blessed the people in the name of the Lord of hosts.

David distributed a loaf of bread, a [?], and a piece of flat cake to each person among all the people from every part of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, both men and women. Then all the people went home, each to their own house.

David returned and blessed his household. Michal, Saul’s daughter, came out to meet David and bless him, saying, “How the king of Israel has honored himself today! Today he exposed himself in front of his servants’ female slaves, just as one of the dancers openly exposes himself!”

David said to Michal, “I will dance before the Lord. Blessed is the Lord, who chose me over your father and over his entire household to appoint me ruler over his people Israel. I will laugh and dance before the Lord.
“I will expose myself again in this way and become like a weak man in your eyes. And as for the other female slaves you spoke about, I was honored in their eyes.”
Michal, Saul’s daughter, had no child until the day of her death.
When the king had settled in his house, the Lord gave him complete rest from all his enemies around him.
The king said to Nathan the prophet, “Look, I live in a house of cedar, but the ark of God lives in the middle of a tent.”
Nathan said to the king, “Go and do everything you have in mind, because the Lord is with you.”
That night the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying to him:
“Go and tell my servant David, ‘This is what the Lord says: You are not the one who will build my house for me to live in.
“‘For I have not lived in a house from the day I brought the children of Israel out of Egypt until this very day. Instead, I have moved about in covered shelters and tents.

“‘In the activities, in all the places where I went with all Israel, did I ever say a word to a single tribe among the tribes of Israel, [?] or to the one whom I commanded to shepherd my people, saying, “Why have you not built me a house of cedar?”’”
Now then, this is what you are to say to my servant David: ‘This is what the Lord Almighty says: I took you from the sheep pasture to become ruler over my people Israel.
I was with you wherever you went, and I wiped out all your enemies before you. I made you greatly renowned, like the great people on the earth.

I will establish a place for my people Israel and plant them there, so that they may live on their own and no longer be anxious from now on. Wicked people will no longer continue to oppress them as they did before,
since the day I appointed judges over my people Israel. I will give you rest from all your enemies before you. And the Lord will tell you whether you are to build him a house.
When your days are complete, you will be laid to rest with your ancestors. I will raise up your offspring after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish your kingdom for him.
He is the one who will build a house in my name, and I will establish his throne forever.
I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me. If he does wrong, I will discipline him with the rod of men and with the sword of human beings.
But I will not take my mercy away from him as I took it away from Saul, whom I removed from before me.’
And the house of your descendants will be established, and his kingdom will last forever before me. His throne will be firmly established forever.
Nathan spoke to David in accordance with all these words and this entire vision.
Then King David went in and sat before the Lord. He said, ‘Who am I, Lord, my Lord, and what is my household, that you have loved me so much?
I have not been humbled in any way before you, my Lord, and you have spoken about your servant’s household for a long time to come. This is the law for humanity, Lord, my Lord.
What more can David say to you? Now then, you know your servant, Lord.
You have acted for the sake of your servant, and according to the purpose of your heart you have done all these great things to reveal yourself to your servant,
so that you may be glorified, Lord, my Lord. You are God, and your words will be true. There is no other God besides you, according to everything we have heard with our own ears.

What other nation in all the earth is like your people Israel, whom God went ahead of to redeem as a people for himself? You did this to make a name for yourself and to gain greatness and glory for yourself, driving out nations and dwelling places before your people, whom you chose for yourself out of Egypt.
You established your people Israel as a people for yourself forever, and you, Lord, became their God.

Now then, Lord, my God, establish forever the word you have spoken about your servant and his household, Lord Almighty, our God, so that the household of your servant David may be established over Israel before you. For you, Lord Almighty, are the God of Israel. Now then, as you have spoken, [?] your name
may it be exalted forever.

The Lord Almighty, the God of Israel; and may the household of your servant David remain standing before you. For you are the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel. You revealed this to your servant’s ear, saying, “I will build a house for you.” Your servant therefore found the courage to offer this prayer to you.
Now then, Lord, my God, you are God, and your words will be true. You have spoken about your servant, promising to bring all this goodness upon him.’

Now, then, please bless the house of your servant, so that it may remain forever before you. For you, Lord, my Lord, have spoken, and through your blessing the house of your servant will be blessed forever.
After these things, David struck the Philistines and defeated them. David took the fortified city from the Philistines.

David also struck the land of Moab. He measured them with ropes after making them lie on the ground. He measured two lengths of the measuring rope to put them to death, but those within a full length of the measuring rope he kept alive. The people of Moab became David’s servants and brought him tribute.
David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he was going to restore his control over the Euphrates River.

David captured some of his troops and took from him a thousand chariots, seventy thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand foot soldiers. David destroyed all the chariots, but kept a hundred of them for himself.
The Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, and David killed twenty-two thousand of the Syrians.
David stationed garrisons in Syrian Damascus to keep watch, and the Syrians became David's subjects, bringing him tribute. The Lord kept David safe wherever he went.

David took the gold bracelets, or armlets, which the servants of Hadadezer king of Zobah had made for themselves, and brought them up to Jerusalem. Pharaoh king of Egypt took them when he came up to Jerusalem in the days of Rehoboam son of Solomon.
David took a very large amount of bronze from Nemasbak and from Hadadezer's choice cities. Solomon used it to make the bronze Sea, the pillars, the basins, and all the utensils.
And Toi, king of Hamath, heard that David had defeated Hadadezer’s entire army.

Toi sent his son Jezuran to King David to ask him for peace and to congratulate him because he had defeated Hadadezer, for Toi had been at war with Hadadezer. He brought silver vessels, gold vessels, and bronze vessels with him.
King David consecrated the others and dedicated them to the Lord, along with the silver and gold that he had consecrated from all the cities he had conquered:
from Edom, from Moab, from the Ammonites, from Amalek, and from the spoils of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Sheba.
David made a famous name for himself. When he returned, he killed eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt.
He stationed guards throughout Edom, and all the Edomites became the king's subjects. The Lord kept David safe wherever he went.
He made David king over all Israel, and David administered justice and righteousness among all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah was in command of his army, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahijah was the one who reminded the king of matters.
Zadok son of Ahitub and Abimelech son of Abiathar were priests, and Asa was the secretary.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was the adviser. The Cherethites and the Pelethites, David's sons, were officials of the king's court.
David said, “If anyone remains from Saul's household, I will show him kindness for Jonathan's sake.”
There was a servant from Saul's household named Ziba. They summoned him and brought him before David. The king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” He said, “I am your servant.”
The king said to him, “If anyone remains from Saul’s house, I will show him the kindness of God.” Ziba said before the king, “There is a son of Jonathan whose feet are disabled.”
The king said to him, “Where is he?” Ziba said, “He is in the house of Machir son of Ammiel, who is from Lo-debar.”
Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came before King David. He fell down before him and bowed to him. David said to him, “Mephibosheth!” He said, “Here I am, your servant.”

David said to him, “Do not be afraid, for I will certainly show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will give you all the fields of Saul, your father's father, and you will always eat with me at my table.”
Mephibosheth fell down and bowed, saying, “What is your servant, that you have taken notice of a dead dog like me?”
David summoned Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, “Everything that belonged to Saul and everything belonging to his household—I have given it all to your master's son.”

So work his land, you and your sons and your servants, and bring in bread for your master's son so that they may eat it. But Mephibosheth, your master's son, will always eat bread with me at my table. Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba said before the king, “Your servant will do everything that my lord the king has commanded his servant to do.” And Mephibosheth ate at David's table like one of the king's sons.
Mephibosheth had a son named Micah. Everyone belonging to Ziba's household was a servant of Mephibosheth.
Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem because he always ate at the king's table. He was lame in both feet.
After these things, the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun became king in his place.

David said, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” So David sent his servants to comfort him over his father. David's servants came to the land of Ammon.

The leaders of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, “Is it because David wants to honor your father in your sight that he has sent comforters to you? Rather, he sent them to search the city and examine it—David himself, so that they might search the city and examine it [?]. David sent his servants to you to investigate the city and examine it.”
And Hanun took David’s servants, shaved their beards, cut their garments in half up to their buttocks, and sent them away.

David was told about his men, and he sent messengers to meet them because the men had been deeply humiliated. The king told them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return to me.”

When the Ammonites saw that David's people had been put to shame, the Ammonites sent and hired the Syrians and Rehob, twenty thousand foot soldiers, and the king of Amalek with one thousand men, and the men of Ishtob with twelve hundred men.
When David heard this, he sent Joab and his entire force of mighty warriors.
The Ammonites came out and arranged themselves for battle at the entrance of the gate. The Syrians of Zobah, Rehob, and Ishtob, and the men of Amalek, were by themselves in the open country.
When Joab saw that they had taken positions against him to fight him on either side, he selected men from all the young men of Israel, and they took their positions against the Syrians.
He placed the rest of the troops under his brother's command, and they took their positions against the Ammonites.
Joab said to his brother's men, “If the Syrians overpower me, you must help me. But if the men of Ammon overpower you, we in turn will help you.
Be strong, and show your strength for our people and for the cities of our God. The Lord will do what is good in his sight.”
Joab and the troops with him advanced to fight the Syrians, and they fled before him.
When the Ammonites saw that the Syrians had fled, they too withdrew before Abishai and went into the city. Joab returned from the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem.
When the Syrians saw that they had fled before Israel, they gathered together.
Hadadezer sent and gathered the Syrians who were on the other side of the Jordan [?], and they came to Helam. Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer's army, marched at their head.
David was told, and he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and came to Helam. The Syrians took their positions against David and fought him.
The Syrians fled before David, and David struck down four hundred Syrian chariots and forty thousand horsemen. He also struck Shobach, the commander of their army, and he died there.

When all the kings who were servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they fled to Israel, made a treaty with them, and became their servants. From that time on, the Syrians were afraid to go and fight on behalf of the Ammonites.

When the year had run its course, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab, his servants who were with him, and all Israel. They devastated the Ammonites and laid siege to Rabbah, while David remained in Jerusalem.
In the evening, David got up from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From his roof he saw a woman bathing. The woman was very beautiful.
The king sent someone to inquire about the woman. He said, “Isn’t this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliab, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”
David sent for her and brought her. He went in to her and slept with her. She had purified herself from her uncleanness. Then she returned to her house.
The woman became pregnant and sent word to David, saying, “I am that woman. Look, I am pregnant.”
David sent word to Joab, saying to him, “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” So Joab sent Uriah to David.
Uriah came in to David, and David asked him how Joab was, how the troops were, and how the war was going.
David said to Uriah, “Go down to your house and wash your feet.” Uriah left the king’s house, and a gift from the king followed him.
Uriah slept at the entrance of the king’s house with all his master’s servants. He did not go down to his own house.
They told the king, “Uriah did not go down to his house.” David called Uriah and said to him, “Haven’t you just come from a journey? Why, then, didn’t you go down to your house?”

Uriah said to David, “The ark, Israel, and Judah are staying in tents, and my lord Joab and my lord’s servants are lying out in the open field. Should I go down to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? How could I do this? As surely as my lord lives, I will not do such a thing.”
David said to Uriah, “Stay here today and tomorrow, and I will send you to Joab.” So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David called him, and he ate and drank in his presence. David made him drunk. In the evening he went out to sleep on his bed with his master’s servants, but he did not go down to his house.
When morning came, David sent a letter to Joab, sending it to him by Uriah.
He wrote in the letter, “Put Uriah where the fighting is fiercest, and withdraw from him so that he will be struck down and die.”
While Joab was besieging the city, he placed Uriah at the place or position where he knew there were strong fighting men.
The men of that city came out and fought against Joab. Some of the troops, from among David’s servants, fell and died. Uriah the Hittite died too.
Joab wrote to David about everything that had happened in the battle.
Joab instructed the messenger, saying, “When you have finished telling the king everything that happened in the battle,
and if the king’s anger flares up and he says to you, ‘Why did you go so close to the city to fight against it? Didn’t you know that they would shoot arrows from the wall?

Who struck down Abimelech, the son of Jerubbaal, the son of Neri? Wasn’t it a woman who threw a piece of millstone down on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why, then, did you go so close to the wall?’ You must immediately tell him, ‘Uriah died too.’”

Joab's messenger hurried up to Jerusalem and told David everything about the battle that Joab had instructed him to report. David became angry with Joab and said to the messenger, "Why did you go so close to the city to fight against it? Didn't you know they would strike you from the wall? Who killed Abimelech son of Jerubbaal? Wasn't it a woman who threw a piece of millstone down on him from the wall, so that he died? Why, then, did you go close to the wall?"
The messenger said to David, "The men armed themselves and came out against us in the field. We advanced against them and pursued them as far as the gate of their city.
But the archers on the wall shot arrows at your servants, and some of the king's servants died. Your servant Uriah the Hittite also died."

David said to the messenger, "This is what you are to tell Joab: 'Do not let this matter trouble you, because the sword devours now one and now another. Intensify your attack on the city, capture it, and raze it to the ground.'" And he encouraged him.
Uriah’s wife heard that her husband Uriah had died, and she mourned her husband.
When the days of mourning had passed, David sent for her and brought her into his house. She became his wife and bore him a son. But what David had done was evil in the Lord's sight.
The Lord sent Nathan the prophet to David. He went in to him and said, "There were two men in a city. One was rich, and the other was poor.
The rich man had very large flocks of sheep and herds of cattle.

The poor man, however, had nothing except one ewe lamb, which he had kept for [?]. He looked after it and raised it. It grew up with him, and it ate his bread with him and his other children. It drank from his cup and slept in his lap. It was like a daughter to him.

A traveler came to the rich man and stayed with him. The rich man was unwilling to take any of his sheep or cattle to slaughter for the traveler who had come to him. Instead, he took the poor man's ewe lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him."
David immediately became furious with the man who had done this. David said to Nathan, "As the Lord lives, the man who did this deserves to die!
He must repay the ewe lamb seven times over, because he did this and had no pity on the poor man."

Nathan said to David, "You are the man who did this! Now this is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: 'I am the one who anointed you to be king over Israel, and I am the one who saves you from Saul's hand.
I gave you your master's house and put your master's wives into your arms. I also gave you the house of Israel and Judah. And if these things were too little, I would give you as much again.

Why, then, have you despised the Lord's word by doing evil in my sight? You struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife to be your wife. You killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.
Now, therefore, the sword will never leave your house, because you despised me and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.'

This is what the Lord says: 'Look, I will raise up disasters against you from within your own house. I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he will sleep with your wives in broad daylight.
For you did this in secret, but I will do this before all Israel and in the sight of the sun.'"
David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the Lord." Nathan said to David, "The Lord has taken away your sin. You will not die.
Nevertheless, you have angrily scorned the Lord's word by this deed, and the son born to you will also surely die."
Nathan went home, and the Lord struck the little child whom Uriah’s wife had borne to David, and he became seriously ill.
David pleaded with the Lord for the little child. David fasted, went inside, and lay down on the ground.
The elders of his household got up and stood over him to raise him from the ground, but he refused to get up or eat bread with them.

On the seventh day, the little child died. David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the little child had died. They said to one another, “Look, while the little child was alive, we spoke to him, and he did not listen to us. How can we now tell him that the little child has died? He might get up now and harm us.”
David saw his servants whispering and realized that the little child had died. David said to his servants, “Has the little child died?” They said, “Yes, he has died.”

David got up from the ground, washed, anointed himself, and put on his clothes. He went into the house of the Lord, bowed down, and worshiped him. Then he went into his own house and ordered bread to be brought for him to eat. They set bread before him, and he ate.

His servants said to him, “What is the meaning of what you have done? Why, while the little child was still alive, did you fast, weep, and stay awake through the night, but when the little child died, you got up from the ground, ate bread, and drank?”
David said, “While the little child was still alive, I fasted and wept, because I said, ‘Who knows whether the Lord will have mercy on me and the little child will live?’
“But now the little child has died. Why should I fast? Can I ever bring him back here again? I will go to him, but he will never return to me again.”
David comforted Bathsheba his wife. He went in to her and slept with her. She conceived and bore a son, and she named him Solomon. The Lord loved him.
He sent word through Nathan the prophet, and he named him Jedidiah, which means “because of the Lord.”
Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David, saying, “I have fought against Rabbah and captured the city of waters.
“Now gather the rest of the people, come and besiege the city, and capture it. Otherwise, I will go and capture the city, and they will give it my name, saying that I captured it.”
David gathered all the people, went to Rabbah, fought against it, and captured it.

He took the crown of Milcom, their king, from his head. It weighed a talent of gold and had a precious stone on it. It was placed on David’s head. He brought out a very great amount of plunder from the city.

He brought out the people who were in it and cut them up with a saw and iron axes, parading them throughout the whole place. This is what he did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
After these things, Absalom, David’s son, had a sister who was very beautiful. Her name was Tamar, and Amnon, David’s son, loved her.
Amnon was so distressed that he became ill because of Tamar his sister, for she was a young virgin. Amnon found it difficult to do anything of this kind to her.
Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David’s brother. And, and Jonadab was a very shrewd man.

He said to him, “What is wrong with you, that you are so pale and ill, son of the king? Now, won’t you tell me?” Amnon said to him, “I love Tamar, the sister of my brother Absalom, and I have not figured out what to do.”

Jonadab said to him, “Lie down on your bed and pretend to be sick. Your father will come in to see how you are, and you should tell him, ‘Let my sister Tamar come and feed me herself. Let her make two cakes beside me, or something for me to eat, so that I can watch her and eat from her hands.’”
Amnon lay down and pretended to be sick. The king came in to see how he was, and Amnon said to his father, “Let my sister Tamar come and make two cakes beside me, so that I can eat from her hands.”
And David sent word to Tamar at her house, saying to her, “Go to the house of your brother Amnon and prepare something for him to eat.”
Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took the dough, kneaded it, made the cakes beside him, and baked them.
She took the pan and emptied it out before him, but he would not eat. Amnon said, “Send everyone away from me.” And everyone left him there.
He said to Tamar, “Bring what I am to eat into the bedroom, so that I can eat it from your hand.” Tamar brought the cakes into the bedroom to her brother Amnon.
She brought them to him to eat, but he pulled her toward him and said to her, “Come and sleep with me, my sister.”
She said to him, “No, my brother! Do not violate me, because such things are not done in Israel. Do not commit this outrage.
And where will I find my disgrace? You yourself will become like one of the fools in Israel. So now speak to the king, for you know that he will not withhold me from you.”
Amnon would not listen to her voice. Instead, he overpowered her, slept with her, and violated her.

Then Amnon hated her with an exceedingly great hatred. The hatred with which he hated her was intense; his later malice was greater than when he had loved her. Amnon said to her, “Get up and go away!”
Tamar said to him, “You have brought this great foul disgrace upon me, doing to me more than [?], and you tell me, ‘Get up and go away!’” But Amnon would not listen to her.
Instead, he called his servant who was in charge of his house and said to him, “Take this woman and throw her out of my presence, outside, and shut the door behind her.”
She was wearing a robe of patterned fine linen, for this was the kind of outer clothing that the king’s virgin daughters wore. His servant dragged her away from him and shut the door behind her.
Tamar took ashes and put them on her head. She seized the robe of [?] that she was wearing and tore it. She put her hands on her head and walked away, crying aloud.

Her brother Absalom said to her, “Was it your brother Amnon who was with you? Now be quiet, my sister. He is your brother. Do not keep this matter in your heart and dwell on it.” And Tamar stayed in the house of her brother Absalom, living as a widow, desolate.
King David heard about all these things and became very angry. But he did not distress his son Amnon, because he loved him, since he was his firstborn.
Absalom did not speak to Amnon, either badly or kindly. Absalom hated Amnon because he had violated his sister Tamar.
Two full years passed. Absalom’s sheep were being shorn at Baal-hazor, near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king’s sons.
Absalom came before the king and said to him, “Look, your servant’s sheep are being shorn. So let the king come with his sons to your servant’s feast.”
The king said to Absalom, “No, my son. Do not have us all get up and come with you, or we will be a burden to you.” Absalom urged him, but the king would not go. Instead, he blessed him.
Absalom said to him, “If you will not agree to come, let my brother Amnon come with me.” The king said to him, “Why should Amnon come with you?”
Absalom pressed him, and he sent Amnon and all the king’s sons with him. Absalom prepared a royal feast.

Absalom gave orders to his servants, saying, “Watch carefully. When Amnon’s heart is merry with wine and I tell you, ‘Strike him,’ kill him. Do not be afraid of him, because I am the one commanding you. Be strong and act like brave men.”
Absalom’s servants did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded them. Then all the king’s sons got up, each mounted his mule, and they rushed away and fled.
While they were fleeing along the road, the news reached the king: “Absalom has struck down all the king’s sons, and not one of them has survived.”
The king got up, took hold of his garments and tore them, threw himself to the ground, and lay there. All his other servants who stood before him also took hold of their garments and tore them.

But Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah, answered the king, saying, “My lord must not say that Absalom has killed all the servants who are the king’s sons. Only Amnon has died, for Absalom had spoken of doing this to him ever since the day he humiliated his sister Tamar.”
“So now, my lord the king must not take this matter to heart, saying, ‘The king’s sons have died.’ Only Amnon has died.”

Absalom fled. The servant who was the king’s lookout raised his eyes and looked, and there was a large crowd coming toward him along the road beside the mountain, at the descent. The lookout informed the king, saying, “Look, I have seen people on the road from Horonaim, beside the mountain.”
Jonadab said to the king, “Look, the king’s sons have come. It has happened just as your servant said.”
When he finished speaking, the king’s sons arrived. They raised their voices and wept, and the king himself and his servants also wept very bitterly.
But Absalom fled and went to Talmai son of Ammihud, the king of Geshur, in the land of Maacah. King David mourned for his son every day.
Absalom fled; he fled to Geshur and stayed there for three years.
The king stopped going out to search for Absalom to kill him, because he had been comforted concerning Amnon’s death.
When Joab son of Zeruiah learned that the king’s heart was troubled over Absalom,

Joab sent to Tekoa and brought a wise woman from there. He said to her, “Act as though you are mourning. Put on mourning clothes, and do not anoint yourself with oil. Be like a woman who has been mourning for someone who died many days ago.”
“Go to the king and speak before him according to these instructions.” And Joab put his words in her mouth.
The woman from Tekoa went in to the king, fell to the ground, bowed before him, and said, “Save me, O king! Save me!”
The king said, “What trouble has overtaken you?” She said, “Indeed, I am a widow; my husband has died.”

“Your servant had two sons. They began fighting with each other in the field, and there was no one to come between them and separate them. One of them raised his hand against his brother, struck him, and killed him.”

The whole clan, or the leading men of the city, rose up against your servant, saying to her, “Hand over [?] the one who killed his brother, so that we may destroy him in exchange for the life of the one he killed, and remove the heir from among you.” They will extinguish my coal, or the other light he left me, so that no memory of my husband, no surviving descendant or name, remains on the face of the earth.
The king said to her, “Go home safely, and I will give orders concerning you.”
The woman from Tekoa said, “My lord the king, let the guilt rest on me and on my father’s household. But let the king and your glorious throne be innocent.”
The king said to her, “Whoever troubles you, bring him to me, and he will not trouble you again.”

The woman said before the king, “Let my lord the king remember the Lord his God, to restrain the one who comes against me to avenge blood, so that he does not destroy him and they do not remove my son from our midst.” David said to her, “As the Lord lives, not a single hair from your son’s head will fall to the ground.”
The woman said before the king, “Let me, your servant, have the opportunity to say a word to my lord.” The king said, “Speak.”

The woman said, “Why have you thought of such a thing against the people of God? Or does this word come from the king’s mouth as a sin, since the king does not bring back the one who belongs to him and has been banished?”

“For we must surely die, and we are like water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered up. Likewise, God will not take the life of the one who plans to banish from his presence the person he has banished.”

Now, then, this is the matter I came to speak about to my lord the king: the people will see me and speak. But let your servant, who is myself, speak with the king, for perhaps the king will act on his servant’s request.
“For the king will listen and rescue his servant from the hand of the man who seeks to cast me and my other son out of God’s inheritance.”
The woman said again, “May the word of my lord the king be right, for my lord the king is like an angel of God, able to hear both good and evil. And the Lord your God will be with you.”
The king answered the woman, “Do not hide from me what I am going to ask you.” The woman said to him, “Let my lord the king speak.”

The king said to her, “Is Joab’s hand involved with you in this matter?” The woman said before the king, “As you live, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right or to the left from anything my lord the king has said. Your servant Joab was the one who instructed me, and he put all these words into your servant’s mouth.
Your servant Joab did this to establish the course of this matter. My lord the king is wise, with the wisdom of an angel of God, so that he knows everything that happens in the land.”
The king said to Joab, “Look, I have done what you asked. Go and bring back the young man Absalom.”

Joab fell to the ground before him, bowed down, and blessed the king. Joab said before him, “Today your servant knows that I have found favor with you, my lord the king, because my lord the king has granted his servant’s request.”
Joab got up, went to Geshur, and brought Absalom up to Jerusalem.
The king said to Joab, “Let him go to his own house and not come in.” So Absalom went to his own house and did not see the king’s face.
In all Israel there was no man like Absalom for beauty or so highly praised. From the soles of his feet to the top of his head, there was no blemish on him.

He would cut his hair at appointed intervals, from time to time, arranging to cut it when it had grown long on him. Whenever he cut the hair of his head, he weighed it, and it weighed a hundred staters by the king’s standard of weight.
Absalom had three sons and one daughter, whose name was Tamar. She was a woman of very beautiful appearance. She became the wife of Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, and bore him Abijah.
Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without seeing the king’s face.
Absalom summoned Joab so that he could send him to the king, but Joab refused to come to him. He sent for him a second time, but he again refused to come to him.

Absalom said to his servants, “Look, the plot, or [?], in Joab’s field is near mine, and he has barley in it. Go and burn it with fire.” Absalom’s servants burned the barley plot with fire. Joab’s servants went to Joab with their clothes torn and said to their master, “Absalom’s servants have set fire to the barley plot.”
Joab got up and went to Absalom at his house. He said to him, “Why did your servants set fire to my plot and burn it?”

Absalom said to Joab, “I sent for you once and then a second time, saying, ‘Come to me so that I can send you to the king, and you can say to him, “Why did I come away from Geshur? It would have been better for me to stay there.”’ Look, up to now I have not seen the king’s face. But if there is wrongdoing in him, then kill me.”

Joab went in to the king and told him these words. The king summoned Absalom, and he came in to the king, fell to the ground before the king, and bowed down to him. The king kissed Absalom on the mouth.
After this, Absalom provided himself with chariots and horsemen, and appointed fifty men to run ahead of him.

Absalom got up early and stood beside the road leading to the gate. Whenever anyone had a dispute and came before the king for judgment, Absalom would stand beside each person and call out to him, saying, “What city are you from?” The man would tell him, “I am your servant, one of the tribes among the tribes of Israel.”
Absalom said to him, “Look, the things you say are good and right, but there is no one appointed by the king to hear you.”
Absalom called out, saying, “Who will appoint me as judge over the land? Then everyone who has a dispute or a legal case could come to me, and I would give him justice.”
Whenever a man approached to bow down to him, he would reach out his hand, take hold of him, and kiss him.
Absalom acted this way toward all Israel, toward those who came before the king for judgment. In this way Absalom was stealing the hearts of the people of Israel.
After forty years had passed, Absalom said to his father, “I will go and fulfill in Hebron the vows I made to the Lord.
For I, your servant, made a vow while I was living in Geshur in Syria, saying, ‘If the Lord brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the Lord.’”
The king said to him, “Go in peace.” So he got up and went to Hebron.
Absalom sent spies to all the tribes of Israel, saying, “As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, shout out, ‘Absalom has become king in Hebron!’”
Two hundred men from Jerusalem whom he had invited followed Absalom. They went in their innocence, knowing nothing about the matter.
Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s adviser, from his city, Giloh, while he was sacrificing to his gods. A great gathering took place, and the crowd accompanying Absalom was large.
A messenger came to David and said to him, “The hearts of the men of Israel have turned toward Absalom.”

David said to all his servants who were with him in Jerusalem, “Get up, and let us flee, for we cannot escape Absalom here. Let us hurry, so that he does not pursue us and overtake us, bring disaster upon us, and strike the city with the edge of the sword.”
The king’s servants said to King David, “Whatever our lord the king decides, here we are, your servants, with you.”
The king got up and went out with his entire household, traveling on foot. But the king left ten women, his concubines, behind to guard his house.
The king went out with all his servants, traveling on foot, and they stopped at the distant house.

All his servants were walking beside him, along with all the Cherethites and all the Pelethites. They came up to the olive tree in the wilderness. All the people were passing by him, and all those around him, numbering six hundred men, were standing beside him. All the Cherethites, all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites—the six hundred men who had come to him from Gath—also marched past the king.
The king said to [?] the Gittite and his men, “Why are you also coming with us? Go back and stay, or attach yourself to the king, for you are a foreigner, and you have moved away from Gath.
And if you arrived yesterday, am I to move you away today?”
He was walking barefoot, and all the people with him each covered their heads and walked along weeping.
David was told, “Ahithophel is among those conspiring with Absalom.” David said, “Destroy Ahithophel’s counsel, Lord my God!”
David continued up to the mountain of God, the place where he had worshiped God. And there Hushai, David’s friend, came to meet him, with his tunic torn and his head covered with dust.
David said, “If you come with me, you will be a burden for me to carry.

But if you return to the city, say to Absalom, ‘Your brothers have departed, and your father the king has departed from me. Now I am your servant, O king. Let me live. I was your father’s servant before, and now I am your servant.’ Then you can defeat Ahithophel’s counsel for me.
Look, Zadok and Abiathar the priests are there with you. Whatever you hear from the king’s house, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.
Look, their two sons are also with you: Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar. Send me through them everything you hear.
Hushai, David’s friend, entered the city just as Absalom was about to enter Jerusalem.

David went a little farther along the road outside the city, and there was Ziba, Mephibosheth’s servant, coming out to meet him with a pair of saddled donkeys. They carried two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred measures of raisins, a hundred measures of dates, and a measure of wine.

The king said to Ziba, “What are these things you have brought?” Ziba said before the king, “These donkeys are for the king’s household to ride on. This bread and these dates are for the young men to eat, and this wine is for those who grow weary in the wilderness to drink.”
The king said to him, “Where is your master’s son?” Ziba said before the king, “Look, he is staying in Jerusalem, because he said, ‘Today the house of Israel will restore my father’s kingdom to me.’”
The king said to Ziba, “Look, everything belonging to Mephibosheth will be yours.” Ziba answered before the king and said to him, “May I find favor with you, my lord the king.”
David came to Bahurim, and a man came out from that place. He belonged to the family of Saul’s household, and his name was Shimei son of Gera. He got up and came out cursing David.
He threw stones at him and at all King David’s servants, while all the people and all the warriors walked on the king’s right and left.
As Shimei cursed the king, he said these things: “Get out, you bloodthirsty and lawless man!”

“The Lord has brought back upon you all the bloodshed of Saul’s household, because you became king in his place. The Lord has given the kingdom into the hands of your son Absalom. Look, you are now caught in your own wickedness, because you are a bloodthirsty man.”
Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? I will go over to him and take off his head.”
The king said to him, “What have you to do with me, sons of Zeruiah? Leave him alone to curse me, because it was the Lord who told him to curse David. Who can say to him, ‘Why have you done this?’”

David said to Abishai and all his servants, “Look, my own son, who came from my own body, is seeking to take my life. How much more, then, this Benjaminite! Leave him alone and let him curse, because it was the Lord who told him to do this.
Perhaps the Lord will look upon my humiliation and repay me with good in place of his curse today.”
David and the men with him walked along the road, while Shimei walked along the side of the hill near him. As he walked, he cursed and threw stones at him from the side and threw dust in his face.
The king and all the people with him arrived weary and thirsty. They stopped and rested there.
Absalom and the men of Israel entered Jerusalem with him, and Ahithophel was with him.
When Hushai, David’s friend, also came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, “Long live the king!”
Absalom said to Hushai, “Is this the kindness you have shown your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?”

Hushai said to Absalom, “I will not do that. Instead, I will follow the one whom the Lord has chosen, the one whom this people and all the men of Israel have chosen. I will belong to him and stay with him.
Besides, whom should I serve? Should I not serve in the presence of his son? Just as I served in the presence of your father, so I will also serve in your presence.”
Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give us your advice. What should we do?”

Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Sleep with your father’s concubines, whom he left behind to guard his house. All Israel will hear that you have shamed your father, and the hands of everyone with you will be strengthened.”
They set up the tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom slept with his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.
The advice that Ahithophel gave in the earlier days was like consulting the word of God. That was how all Ahithophel’s advice was regarded by both David and Absalom.
Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Let me choose twelve thousand men for myself, and let me get up and pursue David tonight.

I will fall upon him and catch him when he is tired, with his hands unbound. I will terrify him greatly, and he will get up and flee, along with all the people who are with him. I will strike down the king alone.
I will bring all the people back to you, as a bride returns to her husband. You are seeking the life of only one man, and all the people will have peace.”
The proposal seemed right to Absalom and to all the elders of Israel.
But Absalom said, “Call Hushai son of Arachi too, and let us also hear what he has to say.”
Hushai came in to Absalom, and Absalom said to him, “Should I act according to what Ahithophel has said? If not, then you speak.”
Hushai said to Absalom, “The advice Ahithophel has given this time is not good.”

Hushai continued, saying again, “You know that your father and his other men are very mighty, and they are fierce in spirit, like a bear whose cubs have been taken away in the countryside, and like a fierce wild boar in a wooded place. Your father is a warrior and will not let the people rest.

Look, he is hiding on one of the hills or in one of the hiding places. When he first comes down upon them, he will strike them, and whoever hears about it will say, ‘There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.’
Your father himself is a mighty man, whose heart is like a lion’s heart, [?]. All Israel knows that your father is powerful and that the other men with him are mighty men.
So this is the advice I give: all the people should gather together to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as numerous as the sand spread along the seashore, and you yourself will be among them in glory.

We will come down upon him in whatever place we find him, and we will settle upon him like dew falling on the ground. We will not leave a single one of them remaining, neither him nor the other men with him.
If he flees into a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will drag it into the ravine, leaving not a single stone in it.”

Absalom said to all the men of Israel, “What Hushai son of Arachi has said is better than Ahithophel’s advice.” The Lord had commanded that Ahithophel’s good advice be defeated, so that the Lord would bring all these disasters upon Absalom.
Hushai son of Arachi said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, “This is what Ahithophel advised Absalom and the elders of Israel, and this is what I advised.

Now send quickly and inform David, saying to him, ‘Do not stay tonight in Araboth in the wilderness. Instead, get up and move on quickly, lest he rise against the king and the other people with him.’”

Jonathan and Ahimaaz were standing at the gate of En-rogel. The servant girl ran and informed them, and they in turn ran and informed King David, because they could not show themselves by entering the gate.
But a young boy saw them and went and told Absalom. The two of them hurried away and entered the house of a man in Bahurim. He had a well in his courtyard, and they went down into it.
The man’s wife put a covering over the mouth of the well and spread [?], which is food, over it. The matter was not discovered.

Absalom’s servants came to the woman at her house and said to her, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” The woman said to them, “They passed by today a little while ago.” They pursued them but did not find them, and they returned to Jerusalem.

After those men had gone away, the others came up out of the well, hurried away, and informed King David. They said to David, “Get up now and cross the water, for this is the advice Ahithophel has given against you.”
David and all the people with him got up and crossed the Jordan. By the time daylight came, not a single one of them had been left behind without crossing the Jordan.

When Ahithophel saw that the advice he had given had not been followed, he saddled his donkey, got up, and hurried home to his own town. After giving instructions to his household concerning the things he had said, he hanged himself and died. He was buried in his father's tomb.
David came to Mahanaim, and Absalom crossed the Jordan. All the people came with him.

Absalom appointed Amasa in Joab's place to command his troops. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Israelite, who had slept with Abigail, the daughter of Nahash, the brother of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.
All Israel, together with Absalom, encamped in the land of Gilead.

Now when David came to Mahanaim, to the place where Shobi son of Nahash, from Rabbah in the land of the Ammonites, Machir son of Ammiel, from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite, from Rogelim, were,
they brought ten beds and rugs, ten bronze basins and earthenware vessels for wine, wheat, barley, flour, a quantity of dried roasted grain, beans, and lentils,

along with honey, butter, sheep, and [?] of oil, that is, calves. They brought these to David and the people with him to eat, for they said, “Look, the people are hungry, weary, and thirsty in the wilderness.”
David counted, or inspected, the people with him and appointed commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds over them.

David divided the troops as follows: one third under Joab, one third under Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and the other third under Ittai the Gittite. David said to them, “I myself will certainly go out with you.”

They said to him, “We will not let you go out with us. If we are defeated and flee, they will pay no attention to us. Even if half of us die, they will still pay no attention to us, because we are ordinary people, while you are worth ten thousand of us. So now it is better for us that you stay behind in the city, because you will be a strong support for us and help us.”
King David said to them, “I will do what pleases you.” The king stood at the gate, and all the troops marched out in groups of hundreds and thousands.
The king gave orders to Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, saying to them, “Protect my son Absalom.” All the troops heard the king giving orders to all the commanders concerning Absalom.
All the people went out to the forest to confront Israel. The battle took place in the forest in the land of Ephraim.
The troops of Israel were routed there before David's servants. The defeat was great that day: twenty thousand men were routed and fell.
The battle there spread over the whole countryside. That day the forest devoured more of the people than the sword devoured.

Absalom encountered David's servants. Absalom was riding a mule, and his mule ran under a branch of the great, leafy oak. His head became caught in that oak, and he remained hanging between heaven and earth, while the mule beneath him went on and left him.
A man saw him and told Joab, saying, “Look, I saw Absalom hanging in the great oak tree.”
Joab said to the man who told him, “Look, you saw him! Why did you not strike him down to the ground? I would have given you ten silver staters and a fine belt.”

The man said to Joab, “Look, even if you put a thousand silver staters into my hands, I would not lay my hand on the king's son. We heard the king give orders to you, Abishai, and Ittai, saying to you, ‘Protect my son Absalom.’
If I were to sin against his life [?], this whole matter would not be hidden from the king, for you yourself would oppose him.”

Joab said to him, “I will be the first to do this, and I will not remain weak before you like this.” Then Joab took three spears in his hand and thrust them into Absalom’s heart while he was still alive in the middle of the tree.
Ten servants who carried Joab’s equipment surrounded Absalom, struck him, and killed him.
Joab blew the trumpet. The people quickly withdrew and stopped pursuing Israel, for Joab was sparing the people.
He took Absalom, and they threw him down into a large hollow in the forest, into the great pit. He piled a great heap of stones over him. All Israel went away, each to his own tent.

While Absalom was still alive, he had set up his pillar for himself in the valley, saying, “It belongs to King Absalom,” because he had said that he had no son to keep his name in memory. His name was given to the pillar, and it has been called Absalom’s Hand to this day.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok said to Joab, “I will run and bring the king the news that the Lord has vindicated him against his enemies.”
Joab said to him, “You are a man worthy to bring this news today, but you will bring news another day. Today you cannot go with this news, because the king’s son has died.”
Joab said to Cushi, “Run and tell the king what you have seen.” Cushi bowed down before Joab and left him.

Ahimaaz son of Zadok answered Joab, saying, “Let me also run with Cushi.” Joab said to him, “Why would you run now, my son? Come, stay here, because you are not fit to run with this news. It will bring you no benefit.”
Ahimaaz said to him, “What does it matter, then, if I also run?” Joab said to him, “Then run.” Ahimaaz ran along the road through Kikkar and overtook Cushi.
David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman went up to the top of the two gates beside the wall. He looked up and saw a man running alone toward him.
The watchman called out and told the king, saying, “It is a man alone.” The king said, “If he is alone, he has news to tell.” The man was running quickly toward them.
The watchman saw another man running. He called out from above the gate, saying, “Look, another man is running alone!” The king said, “This other man is also coming to bring news.”
The watchman said, “I see that the first man runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok.” The king said, “He is a good man, and he will come with good news.”

Ahimaaz called out to the king, saying, “Peace!” He bowed down to the ground before the king and paid homage, saying, “Blessed is the Lord your God, who has shut in the men who hate [?] their hand against my lord the king.”

Immediately the king said, “Is my son Absalom safe?” Ahimaaz said, “I saw the whole crowd rejoicing when Joab, the king’s servant, sent your servant—myself—away, but I did not know what had happened to him.”
The king said to him, “Come, get up and stand here.” So he went and stood there.
Then Cushi also arrived. He said before the king, “Let my lord the king hear the good news: today the Lord has vindicated you against all who rose up against you.”
The king said to Cushi, “Is my son Absalom safe?” Cushi said before the king, “May the enemies of my lord the king, and everyone who rose up against you to harm you, become like that young man.”

The king was deeply shaken. He went up above the gate and wept. As he walked, he kept saying, “My son Absalom! Who will grant that I die instead of you, that I be put in your place? My son Absalom, my son!”
Joab was told, “Look, the king is weeping for his son Absalom and mourning for him.”
The deliverance and victory of that day turned into mourning for all the people, because that day the people heard it said, “The king is grieving over his son.”
That day the people slipped into the city quietly, as people slip away in shame after fleeing from battle.
The king covered his face and cried out loudly, saying, “My son Absalom! Absalom, my son!”
Joab went into the king’s house and said to him, “Today you have shamed the faces of all your servants who fought for you today, and the lives of your sons, your daughters, and your concubines,

by loving those who hate you and hating those who love you. Today you have shown that your commanders and your servants mean nothing to you. For today I have realized that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, that would have seemed right to you.

Now, then, get up, go out, and speak encouragingly to your servants. For I swear by the Lord that if you do not go out today, not a single person will stay with you tonight. And know that this will be worse for you than all the troubles that have come upon you from your youth until this moment.”

The king got up and sat at the gate. Word was brought to the people: “Look, the king is sitting at the gate.” All the people came before the king. But the Israelites had each gone back to their own homes.

All the people were talking with all the tribes of Israel, saying to one another, “King David saved us from all our enemies, and he rescued us from the Philistines. But now he has fled from his land and from his kingdom.”
But Absalom, whom we anointed king over us, has died in battle. Now, then, why are you sitting silently instead of bringing our king back to us?” The words of all Israel reached the king.
King David sent word to Zadok and Abiathar, the priests, saying to them, “Speak to the elders of Judah and say to them, ‘Why will you be the last to bring the king back to his house?’

You are my brothers; you are also my bones and my flesh. Why, then, will you be the last to bring the king back to his house? The words of all Israel reached the king. King David sent for Zadok to come to his house, and the words of all Israel reached the king.
And you are to say to Amasa, ‘Are you not my bone and my flesh? May God do these things to me, and add still more, if you do not remain commander in my presence for all time in place of Joab.’”
He won over the hearts of all the men of Judah as though they were one man. They sent word to the king, saying to him, “Return to us, you and your servants.”
The king returned and came to the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, a Benjaminite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
