There were a thousand men from Benjamin with him, and Ziba, Saul’s servant, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants. He made preparations at the Jordan ahead of the king.

They helped one another bring the king across. The crowd crossed over to establish the king’s household and to do what was right in his sight. Shimei son of Gera fell down before the king as he was about to cross the Jordan.

He said before the king, “Do not let my lord the king remember any wrongdoing, and do not take to heart the sins your servant committed on the day my lord left Jerusalem, so that the king should remember this in his heart.
For I, your servant, know that I have sinned. And look, today I have come ahead of the whole house of Joseph to meet my lord the king.”
Abishai son of Zeruiah replied, “Should Shimei not die for this, because he cursed the Lord’s anointed?”
But David said, “What have you to do with me, sons of Zeruiah, that today you act as my adversaries? No one in Israel will die today. Do I not know that today I will be king over Israel?”
The king said to Shimei, “You will not die.” And the king swore an oath to him.

Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came out to meet the king. He had neglected to care for his feet, had not trimmed his nails or cleaned his lips, and had not washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he returned in peace.
When he came up to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, “Why were you unwilling to leave, Mephibosheth?”

Mephibosheth said to him, “My lord the king, your servant deceived me. For I, your servant, said to him, ‘Saddle the donkey for me so that I can mount it and flee with the king,’ because I, your servant, am lame.”
And he spoke against your servant before my lord the king. But my lord the king did what was right in his sight, like an angel of God. Do what is good in your own eyes.

For it was not the whole household that did this, but people deserving death who did this to my lord the king. Yet you placed your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right do I have to appeal again to the king?
The king said to him, “Why do you keep speaking about your affairs? I have said that you and Ziba are to divide the field between you.”
Mephibosheth said before the king, “Let him take everything, since my lord the king has returned to his house in peace.”
And Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and crossed the Jordan with the king to escort him across the Jordan.
Barzillai was a very old man, eighty years old. He had supported the king while he stayed in Mahanaim, because he was a very wealthy man.
The king said to Barzillai, “Come with me, and I will provide for you in your old age with me in Jerusalem.”
But Barzillai said to the king, “How many days remain in the years of my life, that I should get up and go with the king to Jerusalem?

I am eighty years old today. Can I still distinguish what is good from what is bad? Can your servant, who is speaking to you, taste what I eat or drink? Can I still hear the voices of men and women singing? Why should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?
Or is it enough for your servant to cross the Jordan with my lord the king? Why does my lord wish to repay me with this reward?”

Let your servant, who is myself, stay behind, so that I may die in my own town, beside the tomb of my father and mother. Here is your servant Chimham; he will go with my lord the king, and you may do for him whatever seems good to you.
The king said to him, “Let Chimham come with me, and I will do for him what is good in your sight.”
All the people crossed the Jordan, and the king also crossed. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned to his own home.
And the king crossed over to Gilgal, and Chimham crossed with him. All the people of Judah crossed with the king, along with half the people of Israel.

Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to him, “Why have your brothers, the men of Judah, taken you away and brought the king and his household across the Jordan, along with all David’s men who were with him?”

All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, saying, “The king is closely related to me. Why are you angry about this matter? Have we eaten anything at his expense? Has he given us any honor? Has he lifted any burden from us?”

And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, saying, “You have ten thousand men with the king, and I am the firstborn rather than you. I have a greater claim on David than you do. Why, then, have you dishonored me in this matter? Why was my proposal not accepted before Judah’s, to bring the king back to me?” But the words of the men of Judah prevailed over the words of the men of Israel.

There was a man there who was called the son of a lawless man. His name was Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. He blew the horn and said, “We have no share in David and no inheritance in the son of Jesse. Men of Israel, go to your tents!”
All the men of Israel turned away from David and went after Sheba son of Bichri. But the people of Judah stayed close to their king, from the Jordan all the way to Jerusalem.

And David entered his house in Jerusalem. The king took his ten women, his concubines whom he had left behind to look after his house, and they were placed in a guarded house. He continued to provide for them, but he did not sleep with them. They remained shut away, living as widows until the day of their death.
The king said to Amasa, “Summon the men of Judah for me within three days, and you yourself be here.”
And Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the time appointed for his return.

David said to Abishai, “Now Sheba son of Bichri wants to do us more harm than Absalom. So take your lord’s servants and pursue him, lest he find fortified cities for himself and hide himself from our sight.”
Abishai pursued him with Joab’s men, the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the other mighty warriors. They went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.

They were beside the great stone in Gibeon, and Amasa came forward before them. Joab was wearing his embroidered tunic, with his sword fastened to it at his hip in its sheath. The sword slipped out and fell.
Joab said to Amasa, “Are you well, my brother?” Joab’s right hand took hold of Amasa’s beard to kiss him.

Amasa did not take care to protect himself from the sword in Joab’s hand. Joab thrust it into his belly, and his intestines spilled out onto the ground. He did not strike him a second time, and he died. Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba son of Bichri.
One of Joab’s servants stood over him and said, “Whoever supports Joab and whoever belongs to David, let him follow Joab!”

Amasa lay drenched in his blood in the middle of the road. The man saw that all the people had stopped, so he moved Amasa out of the road into the field and threw a garment over him, because he saw that everyone coming along stopped when they reached him.
When he had moved him out of the road, all the men of Israel passed on, following Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.
He came out from all the tribes to Abel in Beth-maacah. They were all in Harri, and they gathered together and came in pursuit of him.
They came and besieged him in Abel in Beth-maacah. They built a siege ramp against the city, and it stood against the wall. All the people following Joab were planning to bring the wall down.
A wise woman called out from the wall, saying, “Listen to me! Listen to me! Tell Joab, ‘Come closer here so that I can speak with you.’”
He came closer to her, and the woman said to him, “Are you Joab?” He said, “I am.” The woman said to him, “Listen to the words of your servant.” Joab said to her, “Here I am, listening.”

She said, “There was a saying spoken in former times: ‘They made inquiries in Abel and in Dan about whether the things established by the faithful of Israel had ceased. They will certainly inquire in Abel whether these things had ceased.’”
“I speak words of peace among the established places in Israel. You are seeking a way to destroy a city, a mother city in Israel. Why will you destroy the Lord’s inheritance?”
Joab answered her, saying, “Far be it from me, far be it from me to tear down the city or destroy it!”

“That is not the matter. A man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Sheba son of Bichri, has raised his hand against King David. He is the one I am seeking. Give me only him, and I will go away and leave your city alone.” The woman said to Joab, “Look, his head will be thrown to you from the wall.”

The woman went in to all her people and, with her wisdom, spoke to the whole city so that they would cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri. They cut it off and threw it out to Joab. Joab quickly blew the trumpet, and each of them turned back and went to his own home. Joab returned and went up to Jerusalem to the king.
Joab was in charge of the whole army of Israel, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada was in charge of the Cherethites and the Pelethites.
Adoniram was in charge of the tribute, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the one who reminded the king.
Jesus was the secretary, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Ira son of Jair was also a priest for David.
There was a famine in David’s days for three consecutive years, and David sought the Lord’s presence. The Lord said, “The guilt rests on Saul and his household because he killed the Gibeonites.”

King David summoned the Gibeonites and spoke with them. The Gibeonites were not Israelites but survivors of the Amorites, and the Israelites had sworn an oath to them. Saul, however, had sought a way to kill them in his zeal for the Israelites and Judah.
David said to the Gibeonites, “What shall I do for you? How can I make amends so that you will bless the Lord’s inheritance?”

The Gibeonites said to him, “Our dispute with Saul and his household is not about silver or gold, and there is no one in Israel whom we have any cause to kill.” David said to them, “Tell me what you want, and I will do it for you.”
They said to the king, “The man who carried out evil against us, persecuted us, and plotted our destruction—let us destroy him so that he will have no standing anywhere within Israel’s borders.
Give us seven men from among his sons, and we will expose them in the sun before the Lord in Gibeon, from the family of Saul, the Lord’s chosen.” David said, “I will give them to you.”
The king spared Mephibosheth because of the oath before the Lord between him and Jonathan son of Saul.

The king took the two sons of Rizpah daughter of Aiah, whom she had borne to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and the five sons of Michal daughter of Saul, whom she had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.

He handed them over to the Gibeonites, and they exposed them in the sun on the mountain before the Lord. All seven fell together. They were put to death in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out beside the rock, from the beginning of the barley harvest until water fell on it from the sky. She did not allow the birds of the sky to settle on them during the day, or the wild animals of the fields to come upon them at night.
David was told what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul’s concubine, had done. And they were released, but Dan son of Joa, who was descended from the giants, overtook them.

David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan from the people of Jabesh in the land of Gilead. They had stolen them from the square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had left them on the day the Philistines struck down Saul at Gilboa.
He brought the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan up from there. He also gathered the bones of those who had been exposed in the sun.

He buried the bones of Saul, the bones of his son Jonathan, and the bones of the others who had been exposed in the sun in the land of Benjamin, at [?], in the tomb of his father Kish. They did everything the king had commanded them, and God listened and had mercy on the land.
War broke out between the Philistines and Israel. David went out with his servants, and they fought the Philistines. David became distressed.
Ishbi-benob, who was among the sons of Rapha, descended from the giants, had a spear weighing three hundred staters of bronze. He was equipped with a club and intended to strike down David.

Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid, struck the Philistine, and killed him. Then the men swore to David, saying, “From now on you must not go out to battle with us, so that you do not extinguish the lamp of Israel.”
After this, there was another battle at Gath against the Philistines. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, one of the descendants of Rapha.
There was another battle with the Philistines at Gob. Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, struck down Goliath the Gittite. The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam.
War broke out again in Gath. There was a man there named Adoni, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. He too was born to Rapha.
He taunted Israel, but Jonathan, the son of Shimei, David’s brother, struck him down.
These four were born as descendants of the giants in Gath, of the house of Rapha. They fell at the hands of David and his servants.
David spoke the words of this song to the Lord on the day when the Lord rescued him from the hands of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.
He said, “Lord, you are my strength and my refuge, saving me.

My God is my light. He is the one who will protect me; I will trust in him. He is my protection and the horn of my salvation, the one who takes me to himself. He is the refuge that saves me; he will rescue me from the hand of the violent man.
The Lord is blessed. I will call upon him, and I will be saved from the hands of my enemies.
For the pains of death rose against me, and the destructive waters of lawlessness terrified me.
The pains of the underworld surrounded me, and the snares of death rose against me.
In my distress I will call upon the Lord, and I will cry out to my God. May he hear my voice from his holy temple, and may my cry reach his ears.
He looked upon the earth, and it shook. The foundations of heaven trembled because the Lord was angry with them.
Smoke rose in his anger, and fire from his mouth would devour. Coals were kindled by him.
He bent the heavens and came down, with thick darkness beneath his feet.
He sat upon the cherubim and flew away, and he appeared upon the wings of the wind.
He placed darkness before him, with his tent surrounding him. Dark waters gathered, or multiplied, in the clouds of the sky.
From his light the clouds moved ahead of him; fiery coals were kindled.
The Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High raised his voice.
He sent out his arrows and scattered them. He multiplied flashes of lightning and threw them into confusion.
Springs of water appeared, and the foundations of the inhabited world were laid bare in fear of the Lord, at the blast of the breath of his anger.
He reached out from on high and took me; he drew me to himself out of many waters.
He rescued me from the hands of my powerful enemies and from the hands of those who hated me, because they were stronger than I was.
The days of my distress rose against me, but the Lord became my support.
He made room for me and rescued me, because he delighted in me.
The Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he rewarded me.
For I kept the ways of the Lord and did not act wickedly against my God.
For all his judgments are before me, and I have not put his ordinances away from me.
And I will be holy before him, and I will guard myself against my lawlessness.
And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the cleanness of my hands he will repay me in his sight.
When you are with someone holy, you will be holy; and when you are with someone perfect, you will be perfect.
And when you are with someone chosen, you will be chosen; and when you are with someone crooked, you will be crooked.
And you will save the poor people, and you will bring down the eyes of the proud.
For you are my lamp, Lord, and you are the one who will make my darkness light for me.
For through you I will run in safety, and through my God I will leap over a wall.
My God is steadfast; his way is holy. The Lord's word is strong and refined. He is the support of everyone who trusts in him.
Who is mighty except the Lord? And who will be a creator except our God?
The Lord strengthens me with power, and he has made my way straight and holy.
He prepares my feet like those of a deer, and he sets me on the high places.
He trains my hands for war, and he has placed a bronze bow in my arms.
And you gave me the support of my salvation, and your listening to me saved me.
You made room for my steps beneath me, and my feet did not falter.
I will pursue my enemies and destroy them, and I will not turn back until I have finished them off.
I will crush them so that they cannot rise, and they will fall beneath my feet.
And you will strengthen me with power for war, and you will make those who rose up against me bow beneath me.
And my enemies were handed over, humbled before me; the others who hate me, you killed.
They will cry out, but no help will come to them. They cried out to the Lord, and he did not listen to them.
I crushed them like the dust of the earth; I scattered them like the mud of the streets.
You will rescue me from the strife of the peoples. You will protect me, making me head over the peoples and the nations. A people I did not know became my servants.
They listened to me and turned their ears toward me. Foreigners lied to me.
Foreigners will cast themselves out, and they will grow weak from their travels.
The Lord lives, and blessed is the one who protects me. My God, who watches over my salvation, will be exalted.
The Lord is steadfast, giving me vengeance and teaching the peoples to be watchful.
He brings me out from among my enemies, and you will take me away from those who rise up against them. You are the one who will rescue me from a violent man.
Therefore I will praise you, Lord, among the nations, and I will sing to your name.
He increases the deliverance of his king and shows mercy to his anointed one, David, and to his descendants forever.
And these are David’s last words: David the son of Jesse is faithful, and the man whom the Lord raised up over his people Jacob is faithful, and the psalms of Israel are sweet.
It was the Spirit of the Lord who spoke within me, and his word was over my people.
The God of Israel said—the one who watches over Israel spoke with me—“Speak a parable about a man: How will you establish the fear of Christ?”
And in the light of God, when the sun rises in the morning, and like a plant growing up from the earth after the rain.

For my house is not like this with the steadfast God. He established an everlasting covenant for me, prepared and guarded at all times, because all my salvation and all my words are in the Lord, because the lawless person will not grow.
For they are all like a thorn bush that is thrown away, because they cannot be grasped with the hands.
And the man will suffer among them, and all the iron and the shaft of a spear [?]. He will burn them with fire, and they will lay down their shame.

These are the names of David’s mighty warriors: Jebosheth the Canaanite, who was the leader over the three, and Adino the Azonite. For he drew his sword against three hundred men and killed them at one time.

And after him was Eleazar, the son of his father’s brother, the son of Sosi, who was among David’s three mighty warriors when he taunted the Philistines at Hressa, where they had gathered for battle. And the man of Israel cried out.

He was the one who stood up and struck the Philistines until his hand grew tired from striking and his hand clung to the sword’s handle. The Lord brought about a great deliverance that day, while the people were behind him, plundering.
After him was Shammah the son of Asa, the Aruchite. The Philistines gathered at the settlement, where there was a plot of farmland full of lentils, and the people fled before the Philistines.
He stood in the middle of the plot and defended it, and he struck the Philistines. The Lord brought about a great deliverance.

And three came up from the three divisions, or from the three [?]. They came up to Cazon, to David, to the cave of Adullam, and a division of the Philistines stationed themselves in the Valley of Rephaim.
David was in the stronghold, and the Philistine force was in Bethlehem.
David felt a longing and said, “Who will give me water to drink from the well in Bethlehem, the one by the gate?” The Philistine forces were in Bethlehem.

The three mighty warriors set out and broke into the camp. They drew water from the well of Bethlehem, the one at the gate, and took [?] and came to David. He did not want to drink it, but poured it out before the Lord.

He said, “Keep me from this, Lord! May I never do such a thing! Would I drink the blood of these men who risked their lives and went running?” He refused to drink it. These were the things the three mighty warriors did.

And Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was also a leader among the three. He was the one who raised his spear against three hundred men and killed them, and his name was renowned among the three.
He was distinguished among those three and became their leader, but he did not attain the standing of these three.

And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was a strong man, accomplished in many deeds, distinguished among the three, from Kabzeel. He was the one who struck down the two sons of Ariel from Moab, and he was the one who went down and struck the lion in the middle of the pit on a winter day.

He also struck down the Egyptian, a man remarkable to look at. The Egyptian held a spear like a weaver’s beam. Benaiah went out against him with the spear he held, snatched the spear from the Egyptian’s hand, and killed him with his own spear.
These are the things Benaiah son of Jehoiada did. His name was also among the three great warriors.
He was distinguished among the three, but he did not attain the rank of the three. David appointed him to his service. These are the names of King David’s warriors.
Asahel, Joab’s brother, was counted among the four; Elhanan son of Dodi, his father’s brother, from Bethlehem;
Shammah the Harodite; Elika the Harodite.
Helez the Paltite; Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite.
Abiezer the Anathothite, from among the sons of the Pasothite;
Zalmon the Ahohite; Moore the Netophathite;
Ittai son of Ribai, from Gibeah, a son of Benjamin;
the Ephrathite;
Azmaveth the Saraabite;
Emasu the Shaalbonite; the sons of Jashen; Jonathan;
Shammah the Harodite; Hamnan son of Sare the Arathurite;
Eliphelet son of Asbites, son of Maachaachi; Eliab son of Ahithophel the Gilonite;
Hezrai the Carmelite, son of Uri, who is Erchri;
Gilead son of Nathan, who was the son of a warrior, the son of Gileaddi;
Eli the Hammanite; Gelori the Kerothite, who carried the armor of Joab son of Zeruiah;
the Ithrite; Gareb the Iethinite;
Uriah the Hittite. All these numbered thirty-seven.
Eada was from Chimarron; Gabiel, son of the Parabothite.
The Lord’s anger again flared up against Israel, and it incited David against them, saying, “Go and count Israel and Judah.”

The king said to Joab, the commander of his army, who was with him, “Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and count the people, so that I may know their number—how many people there are.”
Joab said before the king, “May the Lord your God increase the people again and again, a hundredfold, while the eyes of my lord the king look on. But why does my lord the king seek to do this thing?”
But the king’s command prevailed over the objections of Joab and the other army commanders. Joab and the other army commanders went out from the king’s presence to count the people of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan and came to Aroer, to the right of the city in the middle of the valley of Gad, and to Eliezer.
They came to Gilead, to Thabason, to Hesthon, and to Adasai. They came to Danida and Udan, and went around to Sidon.
They came to the fortress of Tyre and to all the cities of the Hivites and the Canaanites. They came to the land of Judah, to Beersheba.
They went throughout the whole land. After this, at the end of nine months and twenty days, they came to Jerusalem.
Joab gave the king the count of the people. Israel numbered eight hundred thousand mighty men who carried swords, and the men of Judah numbered five hundred thousand fighting men.

David's conscience troubled him after he had counted the people. David said before the Lord, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done. Now, Lord, forgive your servant's wrongdoing, for I have acted very foolishly.”
David rose early in the morning, and the word of the Lord came to Gad the prophet, the seer,
telling him to go to David and say to him, “This is what the Lord says: ‘I will send three things upon you. Choose one of them for yourself, and I will do it to you.’”

Gad the prophet went in to David and told him, “Choose one of these things for yourself to happen: either famine will overtake you for three years in the land, or you will spend three months fleeing from your enemies as they pursue you, or there will be a plague in your land for three days. Now consider and decide what answer I should give to the one who sent me to you.”

David said to Gad the prophet, “The things you have said are very distressing to me indeed. I will choose instead to fall into the Lord’s hand, because his mercies are very great. I do not want to fall into human hands.”

David chose for the plague to strike him. It was the time of the wheat harvest. The Lord commanded a plague to come upon Israel from morning until the time of the midday meal. Wrath burned against the people, and seventy thousand people died, from Dan as far as Beersheba.

The angel of the Lord stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it. The Lord was implored concerning this evil, or this affliction, and he said to the angel who was killing among the people, “The destruction that has happened is great. Now withdraw your hand.” The angel of the Lord was standing beside the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When David saw the angel, he said before the Lord, “Look, I am the one who sinned. I, the shepherd, have committed wrongdoing. But these are sheep; they have done nothing themselves. Now, Lord, let your hand come down upon me and upon my father's household.”
Gad the prophet came to David that day and said to him, “Get up and go up. Establish a covenant with the Lord and build an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”
David rose and went up according to Gad's word, as the Lord had commanded him.
Araunah looked and saw the king and his servants coming toward him. Araunah went out, fell facedown, and bowed before King David.

Araunah said to him, “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” David said to him, “I have come to buy your threshing floor from you, so that I may build an altar to the Lord and the fury of the plague may cease against the people.”

Araunah said to David, “Let my lord the king take it and do before the Lord what seems good to him. Here are the oxen for you to offer as a burnt offering, and here are the wheels and the oxen's equipment to use as wood for the burnt offering.”
Araunah gave all these things to the king. Araunah said to the king, “May the Lord your God bless you.”

But the king said to Araunah, “I will not take them for nothing. Instead, I will buy them from you for money. I will not offer a burnt offering to the Lord my God free of charge.” David bought the threshing-floor site and the oxen from Araunah for fifty silver staters.

David built an altar to the Lord in that place and offered a burnt offering and peace offerings on it. And he continued to offer up [?] Solomon on the altar afterward, because the work was too small to offer it up at first. The Lord turned his attention to the land, and the fury of the plague ceased there against Israel.
